notes: Interim stay application on LSC General Civil Contract clause 23; arbitration agreement scope and one-stop adjudication are clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: Legal aid contract dispute: stay for arbitration under clause 23
key_facts: Asghar & Co and its partners sued the Legal Services Commission and the Law Society over an unannounced March 2004 raid on their offices during an alleged Official Investigation.
The LSC applied to stay the action, invoking clause 23 of the General Civil Contract, which provides internal review, review, mediation and arbitration.
Claimants alleged conspiracy, misfeasance, trespass, conversion and Article 8 breaches arising from document removal and the investigation.
The core dispute was whether the LSC lawfully initiated and conducted an Official Investigation and acted in good faith under the contract.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application by the LSC for a stay of proceedings pending arbitration under the legal aid contract dispute resolution clause.
enrichment.outcome: Stay granted in respect of all claims against the LSC; arbitrator held to have jurisdiction over contractual and closely connected non-contractual claims.
enrichment.ratio: Clause 23 imposes a binding obligation to refer disputes concerning alleged breaches of the contract to arbitration once internal review and Contract Review Body stages are engaged; the phrase 'disputes concerning alleged breaches of this Contract' is wide enough to cover tort claims whose central issue is whether the LSC breached the contract, giving the arbitrator one-stop jurisdiction.
legal_issues: Whether clause 23 creates a binding arbitration agreement or merely an optional dispute resolution mechanism
Whether the subject matter of arbitration is limited to Contract Review Body decisions
Whether non-contractual claims are within the arbitrator's jurisdiction
Effect of an LSC official's letter disclaiming contractual dispute resolution for validity of the investigation

confidence.notes: Stay outcome, clause 23 construction and scope of arbitration jurisdiction are explicit. Law Society claims and full merits were not decided.

notes: High-profile Chagos compensation permission judgment; renunciation, limitation and tort liability analyses are detailed and authoritative.

enrichment.short_title: Chagos islanders: permission to appeal on compensation refused
key_facts: Former Chagos islanders and descendants sought damages and declaratory relief for enforced removal from the BIOT between 1967 and 1973 to make way for the Diego Garcia base.
Ouseley J struck out claims in misfeasance, unlawful exile and deceit; the Court of Appeal heard an application for permission to appeal.
Most claimants signed 1982–83 renunciation forms on receipt of compensation from the Ilois Trust Fund after the Vencatessan settlement.
Bancoult had already held the 1971 Immigration Ordinance ultra vires, but private law remedies against the Crown remained contested.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal against strike-out of Chagos islanders' compensation and related tort claims.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; signed renunciations bar most claimants and remaining causes of action and limitation defences would in any event fail.
enrichment.ratio: Claimants who signed quittance forms bindingly compromised their compensation claims; the English common law does not treat the Crown as a direct tortfeasor apart from vicarious liability under the Crown Proceedings Act and HRA claims, so misfeasance, exile and most deceit claims are unsustainable; limitation, unconscionability, disability and concealment arguments cannot overcome the 1975–1983 settlement history.
legal_issues: Whether 1982 renunciation forms bar present compensation claims
Whether the state can be sued directly for exile, misfeasance and deceit
Whether deceit extends to false statements made to third parties
Whether the Mauritius Constitution continued in force in BIOT
Whether limitation, disability or deliberate concealment defeats the defendants' limitation defence
linked_authorities: R (Bancoult) v Secretary of State for Foreign and Commonwealth Affairs [2001] QB 1067
Three Rivers DC v Bank of England (No 3) [2003] 2 AC 1
Johnson v Gore Wood & Co [2002] 2 AC 1
Cave v Robinson Jarvis & Rolf [2002] 2 WLR 1107

confidence.notes: Permission decision and principal legal reasoning on renunciation, tort and limitation are comprehensive. Some Mauritius Constitution and deceit points were arguable but held insufficient for permission.

notes: Salvage default judgment set aside; joinder, Part 61 burden and arguable defence on contractual basis are clearly decided.

enrichment.short_title: Selby Paradigm salvage: underwriters join and set aside default
key_facts: Humber Work Boats claimed about £102,000 for salvage after re-floating the barge Selby Paradigm, which sank at Hull in August 2001 following failed temporary repairs.
Default judgment in rem was entered against the owner in May 2003 after the owner failed to defend.
Hull underwriters sought joinder, set-aside of the default judgment and permission to defend, contending the policy was avoided for non-disclosure and unseaworthiness.
Contemporary evidence suggested the salvors may have been engaged by Associated British Ports rather than the shipowner.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application by marine underwriters to intervene, be joined as defendants, and set aside a Part 61 default judgment in a salvage in rem action.
enrichment.outcome: Underwriters permitted to intervene and defend; default judgment set aside; real prospect of success on merits established and delay did not bar relief.
enrichment.ratio: A default judgment does not remove a 'matter in dispute' for CPR Part 19.2 joinder where an arguable defence exists; under Part 61 the court may set aside default judgment when justice requires and a real prospect of success is shown, not on an appellate standard; underwriters were not estopped from applying despite prior non-participation.
legal_issues: Whether joinder is available after judgment in default
Whether Part 61 default judgment requires a heavier burden to set aside than Part 13
Whether underwriters had a real prospect of defending the salvage claim
Whether delay in applying to set aside should defeat the application
index_terms: Institute Time Clauses Hull Port Risks
linked_authorities: Gurtner v Circuit [1968] 2 QB 587
Wood v Perfection Travel Ltd [1996] Court of Appeal
Rees v Mabco [1998] Court of Appeal

confidence.notes: Procedural rulings and salvage merit points are clear. Judge identity is not stated in the source metadata.

notes: Police injury award JR applying Stunt; execution of duty causation and suspension period analysis are well reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Police injury pension: execution of duty decision quashed
key_facts: Detective Chief Inspector French developed chronic depressive illness after a 1998 fatal shooting raid, criminal investigation, suspension and later disciplinary proceedings.
Dr Cooling, selected medical practitioner, found permanent disablement at 53% and that psychiatric injury was received in execution of duty.
Sussex Police Authority challenged the execution-of-duty finding by judicial review.
Mr French was suspended from May 1998, briefly had suspension lifted in June 2001 but never returned to operational duties before retirement.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for judicial review of a selected medical practitioner's injury award decision under the Police Pensions Regulations 1987.
enrichment.outcome: Decision quashed; matter to be reconsidered by another medical practitioner; police authority recovered costs from Mr French but not Dr Cooling.
enrichment.ratio: Psychiatric disablement caused by disciplinary and criminal processes, or by lack of employer support after acquittal, is not an injury received in execution of duty within Regulation A11; stress from being 'on duty' during investigation does not qualify under Stunt, and an officer who is suspended or never actually performing duties cannot satisfy the widened 'on duty' test.
legal_issues: Whether psychiatric injury from post-incident investigation and discipline is injury in execution of duty
Application of R (Stunt) v Mallett to stress during suspension and attempted return to work
Whether inadequate welfare management during suspension can convert non-duty injury into duty injury
Appropriate costs where the medical practitioner actively resisted the claim
linked_authorities: R (Stunt) v Mallett [2001] ICR 989
R v Kellam, Ex p South Wales Police Authority [2000] ICR 632

confidence.notes: Quashing decision and Stunt-based ratio are explicit. Extensive costs discussion does not affect the core legal holding.

notes: ATCSA detainee MHRT section 74 challenge; R(H) practical alternative analysis applied and bail/SIAC interplay discussed.

enrichment.short_title: ATCSA detainee: MHRT section 74 discharge challenge dismissed
key_facts: Foreign national detainee A-R was certified under section 21 ATCSA 2001 and transferred from Belmarsh to Broadmoor under sections 48 and 49 MHA 1983.
The Mental Health Review Tribunal refused to recommend discharge under section 74(1), finding treatment in hospital necessary because discharge would mean return to prison.
Claimant argued the Tribunal should have assessed discharge by reference to release into the community, not remission to prison.
SIAC had rejected his appeal against the section 21 certificate; a bail application to semi-secure hospital was pending.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for judicial review of a Mental Health Review Tribunal decision under section 74 MHA 1983 concerning an ATCA-certified immigration detainee.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; Tribunal did not misdirect itself; even if it had, claimant's position would be unchanged; leave to appeal refused; anonymity order deferred then to be lifted unless renewed.
enrichment.ratio: For a section 48 restricted patient, the Tribunal properly applies the 'practical alternative' approach in R (H) v Secretary of State: where conditional discharge into the community is impossible because of section 21 certification, it is lawful to conclude continued hospital detention is necessary rather than remission to prison; section 74(1)(b) is not rendered otiose and Article 5(1)(e) is not breached.
legal_issues: Whether section 74(1)(a) requires assessment against community discharge rather than return to prison
Construction of 'restriction order' wording in section 74(1)(a)
Application of R (H) v Secretary of State to immigration detainees
Whether alleged misdirection would affect SIAC bail prospects
Anonymity where SIAC proceedings were not anonymised
linked_authorities: R (H) v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2003] 3 WLR 1278
Secretary of State for Home Department v Mental Health Review Tribunal (PH) [2002] EWCA Civ 1868
A v Secretary of State for the Home Department [2004] QB 335

confidence.notes: Core statutory construction and R(H) application are clear. Anonymity and bail procedural matters are secondary.

notes: Straightforward rates liability JR; charity status evidence failure at magistrates hearing is clearly fatal to the claim.

enrichment.short_title: Non-domestic rates: charity status liability order upheld

statutes_considered.title: Non-Domestic Rating (Collection and Enforcement) (Local Lists) Regulations 1989

key_facts: Tower of Refuge Ministry, a religious organisation using premises in Islington for bible training and meetings, faced about £52,700 in unpaid non-domestic rates.
Islington withdrew mandatory 80% charity relief after discovering a false charity number had been used; liability orders were made in the magistrates' court.
At the liability hearing the Ministry produced only a Charity Commission letter about pending registration, not evidence it was a charity.
Charitable status was later recognised, but not before the September 2003 liability hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for judicial review of Highbury Corner Magistrates' Court liability orders for non-domestic rates.
enrichment.outcome: Application dismissed; magistrates were entitled to make liability orders; no sufficient evidence of charity status was before them; summary costs assessment ordered against the Ministry.
enrichment.ratio: Mandatory rate relief under section 43(6) requires the ratepayer to establish it is a charity using the hereditament mainly for charitable purposes; a pending Charity Commission application and past relief do not suffice; refusal to adjourn was not unfair where no arguable charity evidence was adduced.
legal_issues: Whether the Ministry established charitable status for mandatory rate relief
Whether magistrates should have adjourned pending Charity Commission determination
Whether Islington lawfully withdrew relief after discovering a false charity number
Procedural adequacy of judicial review versus case stated

confidence.notes: Outcome and evidential basis are clear. Permission-stage procedural defects noted but not decisive at hearing.

notes: WorldCom telecom leases appeal; summary judgment set aside on Upgrade Agreement and McKibbin misrepresentation issues for trial.

enrichment.short_title: WorldCom telecom leases: summary judgment overturned on appeal

statutes_considered.title: Sale of Goods and Services Act 1982

key_facts: Primus leased STM1 telecom circuits from WorldCom on capitalised long-term agreements; unpaid 2000–01 rentals and a US$1.2m upgrade charge were claimed after WorldCom entered Chapter 11 in 2002.
Colman J gave summary judgment and refused amendments alleging misrepresentation by in-house lawyer Ms McKibbin about WorldCom's financial strength and insolvency risk.
Dispute over Zurich–Paris circuit specification led to an Upgrade Agreement after alleged refusal to supply a channelised optical interface.
Court of Appeal held Primus had a real prospect of trial on rectification, breach, economic duress and misrepresentation defences and counterclaims.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against summary judgment and refusal to amend defence and counterclaim in a Commercial Court telecom contract dispute.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; summary judgment set aside; amendments relating to Third Agreement, Upgrade Agreement and McKibbin misrepresentation permitted; further amendment issues remitted to trial.
enrichment.ratio: Primus had a real prospect of showing the Third Agreement required rectification for optical/channelised configuration and that the Upgrade Agreement was entered under protest following alleged prior breach rather than as a compromise; Ms McKibbin's alleged statements about WorldCom's viability are sufficiently arguable as inducement misrepresentations to go to trial; accounting fraud by senior management could render such statements misleading even if unknown to her.
legal_issues: Whether summary judgment was appropriate on unpaid lease and upgrade sums
Rectification and breach of Zurich–Paris circuit specification
Whether Upgrade Agreement affirmed Third Agreement or was procured by prior breach or duress
Whether Ms McKibbin's statements amounted to actionable misrepresentation
Apparent authority of in-house lawyer to make representations on financial strength
linked_authorities: First Energy v HIB [1993] 2 Lloyd's Rep 194
Investors Compensation Scheme Ltd v West Bromwich BS [1998] 1 WLR 896

confidence.notes: Appellate reasoning on set-aside grounds is detailed. Full trial outcomes remain undetermined.

notes: PPL Francovich preliminary issues; continuing breach limitation analysis and Clark abuse-of-process rejection are authoritative.

enrichment.short_title: PPL copyright exemptions: limitation and abuse preliminary issues
key_facts: PPL sued the Crown for Francovich damages for failing to implement EU Rental Directive Article 8.2 equitable remuneration while retaining CDPA sections 67 and 72 copyright exemptions.
Preliminary issues addressed limitation, abuse of process, laches and estoppel after over a decade of lobbying and consultation without litigation.
The UK implemented the Rental Directive late and the Commission had commenced infringement proceedings over section 72.
PPL claimed continuing breach with fresh causes of action on each occasion of uncompensated public playing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of preliminary issues on limitation, abuse of process, estoppel and laches in Francovich damages claims for failure to implement EU copyright remuneration law.
enrichment.outcome: Claims not statute-barred for damage within six years before issue; pursuit of claims not an abuse of process; preliminary issues answered in PPL's favour.
enrichment.ratio: Francovich claims for breach of the Article 8.2 duty are tort claims requiring damage and give rise to fresh causes of action on continuing breach and on each occasion of consequential loss; commencing within the limitation period is not abusive merely because judicial review might also have been available; PPL's lobbying did not estop or lull the Crown into abandoning defences.
legal_issues: Whether Francovich failure to implement gives one or successive causes of action
Whether claims are barred by six-year limitation under section 2 Limitation Act 1980
Whether late ordinary action is abuse of process under Clark v Humberside University
Whether delay, laches or estoppel bars the claims
linked_authorities: Francovich v Italy [1991] ECR I-5357
Clark v Humberside University [2000] 1 WLR 1988
Dept of Transport v Chris Smaller (Transport) Ltd [1989] AC 1197
Arkin v Borchard Lines Ltd [2000] EuLR 232
Homburg Houtimport BV v Agrosin Private Ltd [2003] 1 Ll.R. 571

notes: Youth Court section 91 committal guidance; robbery jurisdiction challenge failed, cemetery damage challenge succeeded, voluntary bill discouraged.

enrichment.short_title: Youth Court section 91 committal: robbery retained, cemetery committed
key_facts: Ten youths aged 12–15 were charged with three street robberies at a bus stop; Camberwell Youth Court retained jurisdiction rather than commit under section 91.
Separately, 13-year-old H and two others were charged with religiously aggravated criminal damage desecrating dozens of graves at Charlton Cemetery.
The DPP sought judicial review of the robbery committal refusal; H's mother sought review of committal to Crown Court for cemetery damage.
Divisional Court also gave guidance that jurisdictional challenges should normally use expedited judicial review rather than voluntary bills of indictment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Divisional Court hearing of competing judicial review applications on Youth Court section 24(1)/section 91 committal decisions, plus guidance on voluntary bills.
enrichment.outcome: DPP application refused; robbery case jurisdiction decision not plainly wrong; H's application dismissed; committal for cemetery damage upheld; voluntary bill route discouraged for jurisdiction disputes.
enrichment.ratio: Youth Court committal under section 91 for grave offences requires a real prospect of a custodial sentence of or exceeding two years; that is an exceptional power and non-persistent under-15s should not be committed merely because no detention and training order is available; the review court intervenes only if the Youth Court decision was wrong, not merely different; jurisdictional challenges should normally be brought by expedited judicial review rather than voluntary bill.
legal_issues: When a Youth Court must commit grave offences under section 91
Whether ten-defendant street robbery had real prospect of two-year-plus custody
Whether religiously aggravated cemetery desecration warranted Crown Court committal
Appropriate procedure for DPP challenges to Youth Court jurisdiction

R (C and D) v Sheffield Youth Court [2003] EWHC (Admin) 35
R (C) v Balham Youth Court [2003] EWHC (Admin) 1332
R (M and W) v West London Youth Court [2004] EWHC (Admin) 1144

notes: Clinical negligence trial; breach on ambulance and treatment established and causation favouring survival to age 70 is carefully reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: GP negligence: delayed cardiac transfer caused businessman’s death
key_facts: Sir Christopher Harding, 60, died at home on 13 December 1999 from acute heart failure after GP Dr Scott-Moncrieff attended for breathlessness.
The GP diagnosed possible PE, silent MI or infection but arranged private admission to King Edward VII Hospital rather than an immediate blue-light transfer to St Mary's.
He left the patient for about 50 minutes in his car arranging a private ambulance; arrest occurred before NHS ambulance arrival.
Expert evidence conflicted on whether death was myocardial infarction or myocarditis and on prognosis if promptly hospitalised.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of clinical negligence claim by widow and estate alleging GP breach of duty and causation of death.
enrichment.outcome: Liability established; breach in failing to summon blue-light ambulance, remain with patient and administer aspirin and diuretic; Sir Christopher would have survived with prompt transfer; damages to be agreed subject to court findings on quantum.
enrichment.ratio: Where differential diagnosis includes life-threatening PE or MI, standard practice requires the GP to remain with the patient and arrange urgent hospital transfer by blue-light ambulance unless a private ambulance will arrive within about half an hour; failure to give material information about urgency vitiates informed choice of hospital; on the facts acute MI was the likely cause and prompt transfer to a coronary care unit would probably have prevented death.
legal_issues: Whether the GP breached duty by leaving the patient and delaying blue-light ambulance
Whether aspirin and diuretic should have been administered
Whether death was caused by myocardial infarction or fulminating myocarditis
Causation and prognosis if Sir Christopher had reached St Mary's before arrest
Quantum of dependency and funeral expenses

confidence.notes: Liability and causation findings are detailed. Final damages figure was left for agreement following quantum findings.
